w: 1 Cairo RT1, RT2, RT3: how much root coverage to expect, and the neighbors' margins as the ceiling Hint + live class · 6 questions in the bank Know this Cairo: RT1 (no interproximal loss) about 100% coverage; RT2 (interproximal CAL less than or equal to buccal) partial, about 50-60%, up to the interproximal level; RT3 (interproximal greater) none. The most root coverage any graft can give reaches the gingival margin of the neighboring teeth (the more apical of the two): the graft lives on the bone and tissue beside the root, never on the root. RT2: recession with loss of interproximal attachment, where the interproximal CAL (from the interproximal CEJ to the depth of the interproximal sulcus or pocket) is less than or equal to the buccal CAL (from the buccal CEJ to the depth of the buccal sulcus or pocket). You can see the CEJ interproximally. Expect partial root coverage, about 50 to 60% in cases like his: at best up to the level of the interproximal attachment on either side. The tissue can't be pulled any higher, because there is no framework and no blood supply interproximally to hold it there ("if we know how to fix this, we could ... cure everybody from periodontitis"). His rule of thumb from the live class: on a tooth with more recession than its neighbors, the ceiling of what any graft can cover is the gingival margin of the adjacent teeth, the more apical of the two, whichever graft you use. 2 Which graft by its goal: a CTG under a coronally advanced flap for coverage, an FGG for keratinized gingiva Hint + live class · 7 questions in the bank Know this Covered graft = CTG (connective tissue only). Exposed graft = FGG (epithelium plus lamina propria). Choose the graft by its goal: root coverage = a CTG under a coronally advanced flap (the gold standard); more keratinized gingiva = an FGG. A CTG leaves the band about as wide as it was (2 mm stays about 2 mm) but covers the root and thickens the tissue; an FGG can cover some root, just less than a CTG on the same tooth. The rule for which graft: if the graft will be covered by a flap, it must be connective tissue only. The inner side of the flap is connective tissue, and epithelium placed against it "just would not heal properly." If the graft will be left exposed, not covered by the flap, use an FGG, with its epithelium. In the live class he framed it by the objective. For root coverage, the gold standard is a CTG under a coronally advanced flap; to increase the width of keratinized gingiva, an FGG. A CTG under the flap doesn't change the surface: a tooth with 2 mm of keratinized gingiva and 3 mm of recession still has about 2 mm of keratinized gingiva once it heals, but the root is covered and the tissue is thicker. An FGG left to heal on its own lets the palatal connective tissue induce keratinized epithelium. An FGG can cover some root too (his lower incisor case did several jobs at once: coverage for sensitivity, more keratinized gingiva, the frenum out of the way, a deeper vestibule), but on the same tooth a CTG with a coronally advanced flap gets more coverage. 3 Altered passive eruption: the types and their crown lengthening Live class + review guide · 12 questions in the bank Know this Crown lengthening by type: 1A, a gingivectomy; 1B, a flap with osseous surgery (a gingivectomy alone grows back); 2A, an apically positioned flap without bone surgery; 2B, an apically positioned flap with it. Why Type 2 gets an apically positioned flap instead of a gingivectomy: its band is only of normal width, so trimming would leave too little keratinized gingiva. The flap moves the whole band apically. Active eruption ends when the tooth meets its opponent in occlusion. Passive eruption follows: the mucogingival complex repositions apically around the crown until it settles at the cervical level, near the CEJ (Alpiste-Illueca). In altered passive eruption (some call it delayed passive eruption) that last step doesn't happen: the tissue still covers a good part of the crown, so the clinical crown is shorter than the anatomical crown. Coslet's classification reads it on two axes. The type is the band of gingiva. Type 1: a wider band, with the MGJ apical to the alveolar crest, always. Type 2: a normal band, with the MGJ usually at the level of the CEJ. The subcategory is the bone. A: the crest is in its normal range, 1.5 to 2 mm from the CEJ (the slide: more than 1 mm). B: the crest is within about 1 mm of the CEJ, or at it. All four combinations exist, and Types 1A and 1B are the most frequently encountered. The periodontal options are a gingivectomy, an apically positioned flap and osseous surgery, and the type decides which. A gingivectomy works only in Type 1A: there is a lot of gingiva to trim, and the bone is where it should be, so there is room for the supracrestal tissue attachment (the biologic width: connective tissue attachment and junctional epithelium) and the new margin stays where you put it. In Type 1B you could trim the extra gingiva, but with the bone at or near the CEJ there is no room for that attachment, so the tissue grows back almost to where it was: a gingivectomy there is only a short-term fix. Instead, make submarginal incisions, raise a full-thickness flap and do osseous surgery (ostectomy and osteoplasty) to recreate the same crest-to-CEJ distance at a more apical level. In Type 2 you can't afford to trim tissue, since the band is only of normal width: always leave no less than 2, ideally 3 mm of keratinized gingiva. So raise a full-thickness flap and position it apically, shifting the whole band without cutting any away: without osseous surgery in 2A, where the bone is where we like it, and with osseous surgery in 2B. In a periodontally healthy patient, osseous surgery that leaves a physiologic, positive architecture and no defects doesn't cause disease. 4 Pseudopockets and drug-induced enlargement: calcium channel blockers, fibrotic tissue Live class + review guide · 6 questions in the bank Know this Drug-induced enlargement: anticonvulsants (phenytoin, the most documented), calcium channel blockers (the ones you'll see most) and immunosuppressants (cyclosporine). Plaque is still the primary factor, but the tissue is fibrotic, so it takes a gingivectomy, and maybe a word with the physician about switching the drug. The second is gingival enlargement from medications, a gingival disease modified by medication, so plaque-induced gingivitis is always the primary factor. The three classes: anticonvulsants (phenytoin is the most documented), calcium channel blockers (common blood pressure drugs) and immunosuppressants (especially cyclosporine). The one you'll meet most in everyday practice is the calcium channel blocker. Oral hygiene and scaling come first (SRP only if there is periodontitis), but they won't resolve it: the tissue is fibrotic, with extra collagen fibers laid down in response to the drug, so it has to be resected surgically, a gingivectomy with a bur, a blade or a laser. Despite everyone's best efforts, you may need to ask the patient's physician or cardiologist whether they can switch the medication. 5 Keratinized gingiva: the 2 mm rule, and an FGG left exposed to create it A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this With good plaque control KG isn't essential; with suboptimal plaque control at least 2 mm is needed to prevent attachment loss. To create KG, use an FGG left exposed with an apically positioned flap. A CTG covered by mucosa gains no KG. Is keratinized gingiva needed? A zone of attached gingiva is, of and by itself, not essential for keeping periodontal health and attachment, when dental plaque is controlled and there are no other traumatic factors (Kennedy and colleagues, 1985; Scheyer and colleagues, the AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). If plaque control is suboptimal, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't have optimal plaque control, so a tooth with less than 2 mm of KG is likely prone to recession. That doesn't mean every such tooth needs a graft: it is case by case. Not every patient lacking KG has recession, but lacking it predisposes to it, while a thick phenotype with a wide band of KG resists it. His patient had an RT2 recession on a sensitive tooth with no KG: the site was a plaque trap, chronically irritating the margin and leading to more recession. The goal was to change the quality of the tissue, creating a band of KG; root coverage would be a bonus. A CTG under a coronally advanced flap wouldn't do it: covering the graft with the only tissue there, alveolar mucosa, gains no keratinized gingiva, because mucosa doesn't become keratinized just because it covers a graft. So he used a free gingival graft with an apically positioned flap: a trapezoidal flap (a horizontal incision and two vertical ones) placed apically, and an FGG from the palate, with its epithelium, left exposed so it heals into a band of KG, bringing its own determination to keratinize. Covering it with the flap would deny it that. The palate heals by secondary intention. The graft is held only by sutures, so patients are told not to pull the lip down to look at it every day, to keep a soft diet and not to brush the area while it heals. At three months there was a good band of KG where there had been none, blending with the neighboring tissue (bigger on the apical side), and partial root coverage, as expected for RT2. Her sensitivity was gone, the site was easier to clean and less of a plaque trap, and the phenotype was thicker and more protective. 6 Inflammation causes recession; the factors only predispose A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Inflammation causes recession, by either pathway (brushing trauma or plaque). Thin phenotype, brushing, dehiscences, orthodontics, margins, the frenum and smokeless tobacco only predispose. Two mechanisms (from Zucchelli's textbook). Toothbrushing trauma, especially on thin tissue: the epithelium is abraded, the connective tissue under it responds with inflammation, an ulcer forms at the surface, and with continued trauma the margin recedes. Plaque-related: the same process as periodontitis (plaque in the sulcus with poor hygiene, apical and lateral migration of the junctional epithelium, loss of attachment), here on a local scale on a thin phenotype. "The key word here is inflammation": it is what actually causes recession, and the factors above are predisposing factors that make it happen. 7 The acellular dermal matrix: what it is, when, and why it's covered Hint + review guide · 6 questions in the bank Know this An acellular dermal matrix has no cells or blood supply: always fully covered; remodeled and replaced by the patient's tissue; best for many teeth at once. Treating many teeth from the palate means a large, invasive harvest. When you can avoid that, use a soft tissue allograft: donated human dermis, usually from cadavers, processed to remove the epidermis, the hair follicles and the existing cells. What is left, the acellular dermal matrix (ADM, or ADMA; AlloDerm is one), is a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers with no cells. It wasn't designed for dentistry: it has been used since 1995 for burns, head and neck reconstruction, urology (bladder slings, pelvic floor reconstruction), orthopedics (rotator cuff repair, periosteal replacement) and hernia repair, and in dentistry since 1997, now in dental sizes. It is the most common soft tissue allograft (exam-review guide). Advantages (slide): it eliminates the need for a donor site; increases patient acceptance (no surgery on the roof of the mouth); decreases surgical time; treats multiple defects in one procedure ("quote-unquote unlimited quantities"); achieves esthetic results comparable or superior to autogenous tissue; and is easy to use. Disadvantages (recording): it is "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute to the healing, "like a band-aid." So it must be fully covered by the flap, because it heals poorly left exposed without a blood supply. Over time it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's own tissue (histology shows this). In a more demanding site it can't give the same benefit as autogenous tissue; the exam-review guide's summary is that allografts don't work as well as autografts but have many advantages. 8 Untreated recession progresses; why treat it A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Chambrone and Tatakis (2016): untreated recession progresses, so a recession that doesn't hurt still needs a decision. Exposed roots and lost tissue raise the likelihood of (1) dentinal hypersensitivity, (2) soft tissue discomfort (thin tissue with little keratinized gingiva can hurt to brush), (3) root surface caries, (4) esthetic concerns, (5) interference with adequate mechanical plaque control, and (6) greater susceptibility to inflammatory insult. And recession doesn't sit still: a systematic review (Chambrone and Tatakis, 2016) found that untreated recession defects continue to progress, the margin moving further apical. So "let's just monitor it" because it doesn't hurt, isn't sensitive and isn't in the esthetic zone doesn't mean it will stay the same. Apart from RT3, recession should be considered for treatment when indicated. (Restorative ways to treat recession are for next year's course; this session is about soft tissue grafting.) 9 Thin vs thick phenotype: the probe test and recession risk A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Why it matters: a thin phenotype is predisposed to recession, and recession that is already there tends to progress on it, while a thick phenotype resists it. His example: a young patient about to start orthodontics had a thin phenotype over his incisors, so thin you could see the roots. Orthodontic movement, then years of toothbrushing on top of it, would put him at risk of recession he didn't have yet. So before the orthodontics the phenotype was changed from thin to thick: a trapezoidal, full-thickness flap, a connective tissue graft from the palate sutured over the two central incisors (the teeth most at risk), and the flap put back over the graft to cover it completely. At two weeks the tissue was already thicker, and he was cleared for orthodontics with less risk of recession. 10 Excessive gingival display: the cause from the findings, and its treatment Live class + review guide · 10 questions in the bank Know this A hypermobile upper lip (moving more than 8 mm): Botox, repeated about every 6 months, or lip repositioning surgery, which relapses in close to half (better combined with Botox). A short upper lip has no good options (fillers can mask some); vertical maxillary excess needs orthognathic surgery with orthodontics. Its causes, which change what you can offer: short clinical crowns, because the anatomical crowns are naturally short or, more often, because the tissue still covers part of normal-length crowns (altered passive eruption); a vertical maxillary excess, where the teeth are normal in length and proportion but the maxilla itself is longer; or a short upper lip or a hypermobile upper lip, which moves more than normal from rest to full smile. It can be two or more of these together. The finding that points to each: abnormal tooth dimensions and proportions with gingival line asymmetries (altered passive eruption), an increased lower facial third (vertical maxillary excess), a lip under 20 mm long (a short lip), lip mobility over 8 mm (a hypermobile lip). By cause. Altered passive eruption: crown lengthening, by gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, with or without osseous surgery, plus restorative therapy when the patient's esthetic needs call for it (old restorations, veneers). Vertical maxillary excess: lengthening the teeth can't solve it, except a very minimal excess, because you can only expose crown, not root; it needs orthognathic surgery (a Le Fort, for example) with orthodontics, and periodontics may fine-tune the gingiva at the end. Hypermobile upper lip: Botox, which has to be repeated about every six months, or lip repositioning surgery, which ties the lip down closer to the MGJ but relapses in close to 50%; combined with Botox it does better. Short upper lip: no good options; dermal fillers can sometimes mask some of the display. Luckily it isn't the most common cause. With several causes, combine treatments. 11 Esthetic crown lengthening: sound to bone, as much bone as soft tissue, wait six months Live class · 3 questions in the bank Know this Esthetic crown lengthening with the bone at the CEJ: remove as much bone as soft tissue, so the crest-to-margin relationship is kept, only more apically, and the result stays stable. After esthetic crown lengthening: sutures out at 1 week, provisionals no sooner than 3 weeks, the definitive restorations at 6 months. The surgery went one tooth at a time, starting with a central incisor, then matching the other to it, then the canines (more at #6 than at #11) and #10; #7, the reference, got only a sulcular incision. Up to there it looks like a gingivectomy, but he had sounded to bone and found the crest at or very close to the CEJ, so he raised a full-thickness flap (to the first molars, for access to the bone) and removed bone: the same amount of bone as soft tissue, 2 mm of bone for 2 mm of gingiva, to keep the relationship the soft and hard tissue had, shifted apically, so the result stays stable. An end-cutting bur marks the maximum height of the ostectomy; then the bone is blended like a crown margin, with osteoplasty between the roots, for a physiologic, positive architecture. The flaps were sutured back at the incisions. Sutures came out at 1 week; provisional veneers went on at 3 weeks, no sooner, with no subgingival preps while it heals; the definitive restorations waited six months, long enough for the tissues, the attachment and the bone remodeling to settle, which is why esthetic crown lengthening cases wait six months. Her final veneers are shown at 18 months. 12 Esthetic norms: the smile line, the lip, the gingival line and zenith, tooth proportions Live class + review guide · 7 questions in the bank Intraorally, the teeth and gingiva, mainly to see whether there is altered passive eruption, which can be treated. Gingival line: the canines' margins level with the central incisors' (up to 1 mm more apical is accepted), and the lateral incisors about 1 mm coronal to both. The gingival zenith, the height of contour, sits slightly distal to the midline of each tooth, the canine included; from the front the canine's looks centered only because the canine sits at the corner of the arch. A periodontal probe checks the margins against each other. Tooth proportions: the golden proportion, which the slides show in nature, art and architecture. Seen from the front, if the lateral incisor is 1 wide, the central is about 1.6 and the visible canine about 0.6 (the slides: 1.618 : 1 : 0.618, a 9 mm central with a 5.56 mm lateral and 3.44 mm of canine). A central incisor's width should be about 75-80% of its length: a 10 mm long central should be at most about 8 mm wide, and 70-75% is acceptable, but not a square tooth; 50% is a mandibular incisor's shape. Abnormal proportions with gingival line asymmetries mean short clinical crowns, usually from altered passive eruption. (A worn dentition also gives short clinical crowns, from attrition, not altered passive eruption.) 13 The palate: its layers, the greater palatine bundle, the high vault Review guide · 4 questions in the bank The anatomy to stay away from is the greater palatine artery and nerve, the neurovascular bundle. On the slide it runs about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average palate and 17 mm in a high palate. So a high, deep palatal vault gives the most room for error when harvesting (the exam-review guide's point). There are guidelines for which area to harvest from (premolar, molar) and how far up the palate to go. In the live class: assess the depth of the palate from the start, because it sets how far apicocoronally the graft can extend; the shallower the palate, the narrower the graft. Within those limits you are more likely to hit a tributary of the artery than the artery itself, unless you reach the junction where the horizontal palate meets the vertical. Two ways to harvest a CTG: a trap door, elevating the epithelium and connective tissue together and then taking the connective tissue from under the epithelium; or harvesting the whole rectangle with its epithelium, like an FGG, and removing the epithelium afterwards. The exam-review guide puts it this way: sometimes an FGG is harvested but delivered as a CTG, because that is easier to harvest and heal. 14 The mucogingival tattoo: amalgam, and an FGG to replace the color Live class · 2 questions in the bank The main reason for a metal tattoo in the gingiva is amalgam. When a root canal failed, apical surgery (an apicoectomy) cut off the root tip and retrofilled the canal with amalgam, which is no longer done, and the amalgam can leak into the tissue. His patient had had apicoectomies on four incisors, later lost them and had a six-unit bridge from canine to canine, with the stain over it. The fix is to remove the stained tissue and graft the area with tissue that has no discoloration. The recipient site is prepared split thickness ("partial thickness" on the exam means the same thing), and a free gingival graft cut to a template of the preparation is sutured in. Here the FGG isn't for root coverage or for keratinized gingiva; it replaces the discolored tissue. An FGG leaves a distinct border with the tissue around it, so after three months of healing it was blended in with a laser (a blade or a bur also works). Also flagged in class RT3 is the one type not to graft for root coverage; the other types should be considered for treatment when indicated. Root coverage with a CTG or an ADM: the flap is advanced coronally, tension free, over the graft. Probe visible through the tissue = thin (1 mm or less), prone to recession; not visible = thick (more than 1 mm). Of the traumatic factors (brushing, flossing, habits, foreign objects, caustic medicaments), toothbrushing is the most common. You can skip Restorative treatment of recession is next year's course; this session tests soft tissue grafting. He doesn't plan to hand you a chart to work attachment loss out from: know what RT1, RT2 and RT3 mean and how much root coverage each allows.
